name: Book of Kells
info: The Book of Kells is an illustrated Latin Gospel book made by Columban monks in Ireland or Scotland around 800, named after the Abbey of Kells and regarded as the pinnacle of Insular illumination, now held in Trinity College Library, Dublin.

facts.made: Columban monks closely associated with the community at Iona; as many as twelve individuals may have collabourated, of whom four scribes and three painters have been distinguished
facts.form: An illuminated Gospel book in Latin, mostly Vulgate with some Old Latin readings, in Insular majuscule script on calf vellum: 340 leaves (680 pages), 330 by 250 mm, bound in four volumes since 1953
facts.where: Trinity College Library, Dublin, MS A. I. [58]; a copy of the Faksimile-Verlag facsimile is held by the Anglican Church in Kells
facts.known: ten full-page illustrations; the Chi Rho page; elabourate initials and interlinear miniatures; the portrait of the Virgin and Child; the Eusebian canon tables; the theft of 1007; inclusion in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register

t: The Book of Kells was made around 800 by Columban monks, and its fully developed ornament places it late in the series of Insular Gospel books.

Its decoration is far more lavish than that of any other surviving Insular Gospel book, yet the text has uncorrected mistakes and unusable canon tables, which suggests that its look mattered more than its practical use.
Stolen from Kells in 1007 and recovered under a sod, it was sent to Dublin in 1654 and given to Trinity College in 1661, where it has remained.
dyk: Modern examination of the pigments showed that Murex shell purple and lapis lazuli, long thought to have been used in the manuscript, were not; the woad and lichen used for the blues and purples are strong evidence of an origin in modern Scotland.
ev: The Book of Kells was created in a Columban monastery in Ireland or Scotland
The church of the Abbey of Kells was consecrated after building had begun in 807
The great Gospel of Columba was stolen from the western sacristy at Kells and later recovered under a sod, without its golden cover
The governor of Kells sent the book to Dublin for safekeeping when Cromwell's cavalry was quartered in the church
Henry Jones presented the manuscript to Trinity College Dublin
Roger Powell rebound the manuscript in four volumes
UNESCO added the book to its Memory of the World International Register

sections.origins:
The Book of Kells belongs to a group of manuscripts in the Insular style, produced from the late 6th through the early 9th centuries in monasteries in Britain and Ireland and in continental monasteries with Hiberno-Scottish or Anglo-Saxon foundations. Earlier members include the Cathach of St. Columba and the Book of Durrow; the early 8th century brought the Lindisfarne Gospels, the Echternach Gospels and the Lichfield Gospels, and the Book of Armagh is dated to 807–809. Scholars group these manuscripts by similarities in artistic style, script and textual tradition, and the fully developed ornament of Kells places it late in the series, in the late 8th or early 9th century.

The Abbey of Kells in County Meath had been founded, or refounded, from Iona Abbey, with building running from 807 until the church was consecrated in 814. The manuscript's date and place of production have been much debated. Tradition held that it was made in the time of Columba, perhaps by his own hand, but this has long been discredited on palaeographic and stylistic grounds: most evidence points to a date around 800, long after Columba's death in 597. The proposed 9th-century dating coincides with the Viking raids on Lindisfarne and Iona, which began around 793–794 and eventually dispersed the monks and their relics into Ireland and Scotland. Another tradition, with some traction among Irish scholars, holds that it was made for the 200th anniversary of the saint's death.
sections.content:
The Book of Kells contains the four Gospels of the New Testament in Latin, preceded by prefaces, summaries and concordances. The surviving book has preliminary matter, the complete Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke, and the Gospel of John as far as John 17:13. The preliminaries are two fragmentary lists of Hebrew names, the Breves causae (Gospel summaries), the Argumenta (short biographies of the Evangelists) and the Eusebian canon tables, which were developed to cross-reference the Gospels. The text is largely Vulgate, with several passages from the earlier Old Latin versions, and it differs from the Vulgate in places: at Matthew 10:34 it reads gaudium ("joy") where gladium ("sword") is expected.

The text is accompanied by ten full-page miniatures: the Virgin and Child, three pages of evangelist symbols, two evangelist portraits, Christ enthroned, a carpet page, the Arrest of Jesus and the Temptation of Christ. Thirty-three of the surviving pages carry decoration that dominates the whole page. The opening words of each Gospel are decorated so lavishly that the text is almost illegible, and the Chi Rho monogram at Matthew 1:18 grows to consume an entire page, with animals and insects hidden in its swirling knotwork and three angels rising from one arm of the chi. It is the largest and most lavish Chi Rho in any Insular Gospel book. Peacocks appear as symbols of Christ, because the flesh of the peacock was held not to putrefy.
sections.making:
The book must have been the product of a major scriptorium over several years, yet it was apparently never finished: the planned decoration of some pages appears only in outline. As many as twelve individuals may have collabourated, of whom four scribes and three painters have been distinguished. Françoise Henry identified three scribes, Hand A, Hand B and Hand C, and a fourth, Hand D, has been hypothesised. She also named three artists: the "Goldsmith", who made the Chi Rho page, the "Illustrator", who produced the Temptation and the Arrest of Christ, and the "Portrait Painter", who painted Christ and the Evangelists. The script is Insular majuscule, written in iron gall ink on calf vellum of high quality but uneven thickness.

The palette is broad, with purple, lilac, red, pink, green and yellow the commonest colours, whereas the Book of Durrow uses only four. As is usual in Insular work, no gold or silver leaf was used. The pigments included red and yellow ochre, a green copper pigment, orcein and woad, and the yellow orpiment was exported from Italy. The scribes seem often to have depended on memory rather than on their exemplar, and the order of the Breves causae and Argumenta repeats that of the Book of Durrow, which led T. K. Abbott to conclude that the scribes had Durrow or a common model in hand. Four competing theories place the work at Iona and Kells, at Iona alone, at Kells alone, or at Dunkeld or another Pictish monastery; the first is widely accepted.
sections.reception:
The book had a sacramental rather than an educational purpose. A Gospel so large and lavish would have been left on the high altar and removed only for the reading of the Gospel at Mass, with the reader probably reciting from memory. The Annals of Ulster record that it was stolen from the sacristy, where the vessels of the Mass were kept, not from a library. The design seems to reflect this: numerous mistakes were left uncorrected, lines were often finished in a blank space in the line above, and the chapter numbers that would have made the canon tables usable were never put into the margins, so that aesthetics were given priority over utility.

In the 12th century Gerald of Wales described seeing a great Gospel book in Kildare, which many have since assumed was the Book of Kells, writing that "you might say that all this was the work of an angel, and not of a man". Land charters of the Abbey of Kells were copied onto its blank pages in the 12th century. Its fame as a world treasure began in the 19th century, when its association with Columba was used to demonstrate Ireland's cultural primacy in the debate over the relative authority of the Irish and Roman churches. Queen Victoria and Prince Albert were invited to sign it in 1849, and its artistry influenced the Celtic Revival.
sections.survival:
Kells Abbey was pillaged by Vikings many times at the beginning of the 9th century, and how the book survived is not known. The earliest historical reference is a 1007 entry in the Annals of Ulster, which records that the great Gospel of Columkille was stolen at night from the western sacristy of the great stone church at Cenannas on account of its wrought shrine, and recovered a few months later, without its golden and bejewelled cover, "under a sod". The force of tearing it from its cover may account for the folios missing from the beginning and end. The abbey was dissolved because of the ecclesiastical reforms of the 12th century, and its church became a parish church in which the book remained.

In 1654, when Cromwell's cavalry was quartered in the church, the governor of the town sent the book to Dublin for safekeeping, and in 1661 Henry Jones, Bishop of Clogher, presented it to Trinity College. About 370 folios are believed to have existed originally; James Ussher counted 344 in 1621, and the missing bifolium 335–336 was found and restored in 1741. A 19th-century rebinding badly cropped the pages and cut off small parts of some illustrations, a rebinding of 1895 broke down quickly, and in 1953 Roger Powell rebound the book in four volumes. In 2000 the volume holding Mark suffered what has been called minor pigment damage on its way to Canberra, perhaps from the vibration of the aeroplane's engines.
sections.legacy:
In the 19th century several Victorian picture books of medieval illuminations featured designs from the Book of Kells, which were copied and adapted extensively, so that its patterns appeared in metalwork, embroidery, furniture and pottery. Helen Campbell D'Olier made some of the first faithful reproductions, on vellum with pigments like the original, and photographs of her drawings appeared in Sullivan's study of 1913. The Swiss publisher Urs Graf Verlag Bern produced the first facsimile in 1951, Thames and Hudson a partial facsimile in 1974 with a study by Françoise Henry, and Faksimile-Verlag Luzern a full-colour facsimile published in 1990, made after a process using gentle suction allowed pages to be photographed without being touched.

Trinity College produced a digital copy in 2006, and the Faksimile-Verlag images are now online in its Digital Collections portal. The manuscript is shown in Trinity College Library, two pages at a time, rotated every six to eight weeks. Christopher de Hamel writes that the Ireland in which it was made "was clearly no primitive backwater", and that it is "as uniquely Irish as anything imaginable" while also being a Mediterranean text, with lines of trade and communication unknown to us. In 2011 UNESCO added it to its Memory of the World International Register, recognising it as a globally important historical document.

summary: The Book of Kells is a Latin Gospel book made around 800 by Columban monks, with ten full-page miniatures and ornament more lavish than in any other surviving Insular Gospel book. Stolen from Kells in 1007 and recovered, it went to Trinity College Dublin in 1661 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2011.

George Henderson, From Durrow to Kells: The Insular Gospel-books, 650–800 (Thames and Hudson, 1987)
Françoise Henry, The Book of Kells: Reproductions from the Manuscript in Trinity College, Dublin (Alfred A Knopf, 1974)
Bernard Meehan, The Book of Kells: An Illustrated Introduction to the Manuscript in Trinity College Dublin (Thames and Hudson, 1994)
Edward Sullivan, The Book of Kells (Studio Publications, 1952)
notes: Origin: the article lists four competing theories for place of production (Iona then Kells, Iona, Kells, Dunkeld); the first is called widely accepted, and the facts box says 'Columban monks closely associated with the community at Iona', which the article calls certain.
Date: c. 800 given as start with circa true; the article also says late 8th or early 9th century and mentions a tradition tying it to the 200th anniversary of Columba's death (c. 797).
Folio counts: about 370 originally, 344 in 1621, 340 now; the article says 'another four or five' are missing after folios 177, 239 and 330. Left out of the sections beyond the 370 and 344 figures.
Colours: the article says both that Murex purple and lapis lazuli were once thought used and that they were not; I follow the latter.
The article says the Chronicles of Ulster in one place and the Annals of Ulster elsewhere; I use Annals of Ulster.

Left out: the film The Secret of Kells and the facsimile price and cost details; the Book of Kildare quotation is shortened; George Bain's reading of the John incipit; the mixed art-historical claim that the Virgin and Child is the first in a Western manuscript.
